title: Made in Our Image: A Live Conversation on AI
excerpt: In the output of AI, we see ourselves refracted through a strange new form of intelligence. This issue is an attempt to make sense of those refractions.
content_html:
Big Think hosted a live event on our latest issue, Made in Our Image, which explores the philosophies behind artificial intelligence and what they reveal about us. Executive Producer Dan Hayes sat down with the writers behind the magazine for a candid conversation about the human side of this century’s most consequential technology, along with a behind-the-scenes look at what went into making our favorite issue yet.

DAN: .It's a real point of pride for us at Big Think to produce these quarterly magazines. It's amazing to have a real-life thing you can put on your nightstand or coffee table and read in the real world. The response has frankly been overwhelming since we started. We continue to find more and more people who value big ideas, who are yearning for an analog thought partner, if you will. So shout-out to the whole team who made this possible. Thank you, guys. You're the best.

I have two awesome writers with me today, Afra Wang and Namir Khaliq. Here's what we're going to get into. I'm going to throw 10 or 15 questions at you, just so you have context for where we're going.

We're going to start by learning about the AI-generated film Zombie Scavenger, and what Afra thought she was going to find exploring AI slop and AI content creation in China. At some point I want to ask Afra what the worst piece of slop she saw while reporting this story was. I want to talk a little about the relationship between censorship and art, and what AI slop might ultimately have to do with China's ghost cities. There's an interesting parallel that Afra draws in her story.

We'll also talk through the relationship between Afra's AI slop article and Namir's permanent underclass piece, which I think have some overlapping themes. I'm going to share a little about my experiences with AI as a filmmaker for the group to consider. Then, with Namir, we're going to talk about the idea of a permanent underclass. Is it real, or just a meme on X? Is AI the new industrial revolution, this time for knowledge workers? Is every generation convinced it's living through the end of history? Is it evolutionarily harder for us humans to genuinely imagine real upsides?

Is our nation's character, from Silicon Valley to Wall Street to the American West, built on the virtue of labor? What happens if intelligent machines give us everything we could ever want? What might there be left to do with our lives in an AI-delivered utopia? And the last one: Do humans have a basic need to contribute in order to find meaning in our lives?

Those are some of the topics we're going to explore. You can also put your questions in the chat, and my colleague Claire is going to pop on toward the end to share them. This is your chance to engage with some super smart and interesting people, so please feel free to load us up with questions, and we'll hit a bunch of them toward the end of the hour.

Thank you both so much for being with us today. Afra, I want to start with you. Can you give us your personal background, so people understand how you got into this space in the first place? And please be sure to touch on your brief, dreamlike internship in the film industry.

AFRA: Yeah, of course. I've been a cinephile for as long as I can remember. So when some video generation tools emerged from the Chinese AI space, I got really interested and really excited. At that moment, the whole discourse about the US-China AI race was already happening, and OpenAI had abandoned their Sora project. If you remember Sora, there was a brief moment when everyone could use ChatGPT's newest video generation tools to generate a bunch of slop. One of the most memorable was Sam Altman stealing GPUs from a random shopping mall, if you remember that.

I was really intrigued by the level of creativity AI video generation as a vertical could reach. At the same time, China seemed to have an advantage, in the sense that a lot more video generation tools were coming out of China's innovation space, and a lot more people seemed to want to jump into AI and creativity. Meanwhile, in the West, if you're a reputable director and you dare to say out loud, "I'm optimistic about AI, I want to embrace this technology," you'll probably get denounced by your peers, or feel morally delinquent, because a lot of people are protesting against AI. Unions in Hollywood are constantly organizing anti-AI activities.

So I thought, okay, is this China's big opportunity to forge its own soft power through AI-generated content? That was my sort of 4D chess in my mind. I really wanted to understand this phenomenon, so I got into the space. I talked to many filmmakers, many producers, and many young people in their early 20s who had jumped into this space. I also watched a lot of AI slop myself. I downloaded a bunch of vertical short-video apps and spent hours and hours watching them, hoping to find something touching, something moving, something fundamentally artistic. What I found was this complex, this industrial-scale slop generation machine, which I wrote about in my article.

As for my dream internship: I was a typical first-year college student who didn't know what to do over the summer. I was still a kid. I asked my mom, "If I spend two months in Beijing" (that's where I grew up, where my parents were) "what should I do?" My mom had some connections, and she got me into that internship. It was really fun. I was able to chat with a lot of Hong Kong directors. Beijing was a gold mountain back then. A lot of Hong Kong filmmakers, really the entire industry, were moving north and making Beijing a center of their artistic practice, so there was a big Hong Kong diaspora in Beijing. I was hanging out with a lot of those Hong Kong directors who had witnessed the most legendary phase of the golden age of Hong Kong cinema.

DAN: That's awesome. That sounds like a pretty cool experience. So your hopes for AI film were high, given your background. Can you share the example of Zombie Scavenger? There have been glimmers of hope in what you've seen in China in terms of creativity, and you thought maybe this was the new way forward for AI. Tell people about that film and what happened after.

AFRA: Yeah, absolutely. If you're familiar with Love, Death & Robots, the Netflix short series, Zombie Scavenger feels like one of those episodes. It's a very short piece, about three minutes, but the universe it brought me into was very real and very coherent. It's like how Love, Death & Robots gives you a complete story setting and invites you into a unique storytelling space: something happened in outer space, something happened in the future, something happened in a post-apocalyptic world. Zombie Scavenger is one of those stories. It takes place in a world where humans went extinct because of a zombie outbreak, and the whole story is a romance between a robot and a mannequin.

It's really whimsical and romantic, and it has a lot of interesting motifs from '60s Hollywood movies, from the cowboy genre, and from the zombie genre. It really paid tribute to a lot of familiar motifs we all know. Then I learned that this short wasn't produced by one of those top-notch teams at Netflix. It was produced by a nobody, a 28-year-old nobody from Yunnan province. Not even Beijing or Shanghai, those cosmopolitan cities, but a very distant province. The filmmaker himself is a wedding photographer. He doesn't speak English; he didn't even make the film in English. But in the end, you get this Hollywood-quality output. That became huge news in the Chinese AI filmmaking industry.

DAN: And real quick, Afra, you said it was produced in 10 days for $442. And it led to American filmmakers calling this kid and saying, "You should come and produce stuff with us." So this was a real moment in AI filmmaking.

AFRA: Yeah, absolutely. The film became internationally renowned in a sense. Chinese AI filmmakers were very invigorated by it, and American filmmakers were thinking, okay, China is probably going to have an asymmetrical advantage. A lot more hidden talent is going to flourish because this tool lets people make something like this for a few hundred dollars. I was excited, a lot of Hollywood filmmakers were excited, and there was an effort to scout for talent from Hollywood. I personally know this filmmaker was contacted by a lot of Hollywood producers at the time, and many more young Chinese people were dreaming of being contacted by Hollywood filmmakers. So that was a very optimistic moment, and it got me started on this scavenger hunt through Chinese AI innovation in moviemaking.

DAN: And so then you were like, all right, cool, let's go find all the other cool examples. But basically, you watched 15-plus AI films and tons more shorts, and you felt like you were in an uncanny valley that was terrible. What's some of the worst stuff you saw? And what makes this AI content actually slop? There are blurry lines, so why do you consider it slop?

AFRA: Mostly, the reason you don't feel good after watching them is very similar to why you don't feel good after spending two hours scrolling TikTok. You've viscerally been hacked by the algorithm. Your dopamine is being depleted by the algorithm. While you're watching, you're hooked by very tacky, shocking, dramatic plots. Someone accidentally gets pregnant with a baby by both her husband and her husband's brother. There are certain elements of those dramas that are just subversively controversial and make you want to keep going. And the reason you want to keep going is not good. It's not your artistic curiosity or your intellectual curiosity. It's just that your dopamine has been hacked.

You're like a monkey that's been fed one bite of banana and wants to chase the next bite. I really felt like an animal being harnessed by the algorithm to keep watching, and I honestly don't appreciate that feeling. All those AI slops don't have deliberate or thoughtful plotlines. The plotlines just maximize how much drama can happen within three or four minutes. Then you need to hit the next one, and three episodes later, you need to pay to keep watching.

DAN: I feel like it's not necessarily slop, but even modern YouTube influencer content has a certain characteristic, and definitely a certain pace. As a filmmaker, I can see it's going so fast. There's no space, no breath, because they're just trying to give people that story hit, that bite, to keep propelling them through a narrative. When I watch even modern YouTubers, it's hypercut, and the shots are so quick that I feel assaulted, or just tired watching it. It's kind of crazy.

That's super interesting. And you're saying they're creating this stuff at incredible scale, basically trying to find a hit that makes this economic engine for producing slop viable. Talk a little about the scale of this. Afterward, I want to chat about the ghost cities, and then we'll head over to Namir for a bit.

AFRA: Totally. After you watch enough AI slop, you start to notice that a lot of the female and male faces are converging into a very similar shape. They have very similar layouts of noses and eyes and ears. All of a sudden you think, there must be a vast industry behind this, probably because of economic incentives. So I started to dig in, and, not entirely to my surprise, it's highly tied to China's regional competition.

China has 30-plus provinces, and each province, whether economically advanced or not, wants a share of the most advanced technological development that the central government is signaling to the entire state. Since 2024, Xi Jinping himself has publicly announced many times that AI is going to diffuse into many industries in China. AI is what they call the highest-quality "productive force." This is a very Marxist term. It means electricity was once that, energy was once that, and now it's AI. So Beijing sent a very clear signal to all the local governments and entrepreneurs that AI will be the thing that fuels the engine of China's innovation.

This is basically how China works: Beijing sends out a signal and lets the local governments interpret it and figure out what it means. After the AI Plus initiative was announced, many local governments started to think, okay, how can we participate in this new innovation, this industrial upgrade? How can we not be left behind? How can we have a piece of this strategic technology when we don't have enough talent?

I'm not talking about Beijing, Shanghai, or Shenzhen. Those advanced coastal cities were already participating in the AI revolution. I'm talking about many distant provinces and regions. One example would be Nanjing. It's a city with a large population, but nobody really sees Nanjing as a tech hub or AI hub. There's Hefei. There are many second-tier and third-tier cities saying, okay, we want to jump on this AI bandwagon and create a strategic AI initiative in our region. But what can we do that has the lowest barrier to entry? That's AI video generation. You can just get some compute, get a bunch of young people, plant some seeds in their minds, and have them be creative.

That's an easy, participatory action a local government can take. So many governments started talent incubation programs, where they held public AI video generation competitions to attract people to submit their work and start their own studios. The local government would then give them subsidies or rewards to make the whole space more prosperous and popular. The whole industrial AI slop complex was pretty much a result of this regional competition among different local governments in China.

DAN: So that's one of the reasons there's been such scale and volume in producing this AI slop. By the way, this is all totally new to me. I had no context for the Chinese cultural and policy side of this, so this was a really good educational article. Last question for you, and then, Namir, we'll head your way. You compare this to the ghost cities in China, these huge cities that were built at massive scale but are now empty and full of weeds. Help us understand that analogy.

AFRA: I think it goes back to the downside of regional competition. China's regional competition has its own merits. The reason China is winning the EV race, the reason China was able to produce so many solar panels, the reason China was able to generate so much electricity and harness so much solar and hydropower, is that different regions compete against each other. They want a strategic advantage in certain important industries.

At the same time, you have a very severe issue called overcapacity. Overcapacity is essentially something like a ghost city, where local officials were convinced that building infrastructure was fundamentally important. It's their way of getting promoted, of showing they're diligent civil servants, of being part of China's economic miracle. So everyone started building infrastructure, building cities, inviting real estate developers, and lending a bunch of money for those projects. In the end, China has a tremendous number of unoccupied, vacant high-rise buildings and residential complexes that nobody was able to afford or buy. And right now in China, the real estate bubble has burst too, so the ghost city scenario is even more severe. You drive to the suburbs and see a brand-new city appear in front of you, but it doesn't have many people.

The exact same thing happened with China's high-speed railways. Today, 80% to 85% of Chinese high-speed rail lines are losing money, because many were built to connect distant cities to other distant cities, and there isn't enough traffic to cover the cost.

And the exact same thing happened in AI slop generation. After all this talent and compute and local subsidies poured into the space, you get a tremendous amount of content that nobody is watching. If you understand the YouTube or TikTok algorithms, you know they follow a power law. The top tier of creators, the 1%, occupy maybe 90% of people's attention. The same thing happened on those short-form AI video platforms. The result is a tremendous amount of stuff being produced that nobody watches, and people trying to squeeze out that 1% of good content and replicate it. So you see this homogenizing tendency, where all the characters look very similar, because a similar face was probably in one of the hits from two months ago, and they're trying to replicate that exact face in the next plotline. All these weird, uncanny things happen, and it just isn't a pleasant experience. In the end, I felt like I was venturing into many, many ghost cities. It's just not very good. I think I wrote this out of some slop PTSD. I got really overwhelmed. I wanted a mental cleanse.

DAN: You've got to go watch some classic old films. Watch 8½ by Fellini or something, get yourself out of there. I thought it was really interesting. First of all, I think we should solve the US housing crisis by airlifting China's ghost cities into the US. I don't know if that would work, but maybe if we get big enough ships. But no, this article is awesome. The industrial slop complex, and the design is really cool. So if you members have your magazines, check out Afra's awesome article. Thank you so much, Afra, for educating us on this. It was really, really cool.

AFRA: Thank you so much, Dan.

NAMIR: Can I jump in with a final question? One: Who is watching this sort of stuff in China? Is it young people? Old people? Everyone? No one? And two: Do you have a theory as to why China hasn't been able to develop the same sort of international cultural reputation as even South Korea or Japan, let alone the US? Do they just not have the same internal culture developed as these other places, or what's the cause?

AFRA: I'll answer the first question first: Who's watching AI slop? Everyone, from 70-year-old grandpas to 15-year-old high schoolers. If there's a US-China AI race, I think the US and China are also racing to brain-rot each other's populations. And if there's a brain-rot race, China is probably winning right now.

A couple of weeks ago, there was a huge debate online about compute usage in China versus the US. Some argued that half of Chinese compute goes to AI slop generation, while a lot of US compute goes to R&D, software programming, and AI for science. In the highbrow Chinese AI discussion sphere, people were paranoid about China's overwhelming amount of AI slop, asking: Are we losing our grip? Are we losing our advantage? Why are we using so much compute and inference just to feed AI slop? People in the Chinese AI industry are even having an identity crisis, which I found really interesting.

If you go to China, you'll see that people are a lot more addicted to digital life. People are a lot more interested in going to Instagrammable restaurants, taking pictures, and posting them on social media. That whole activity is much more prevalent. I think that's partly because China has a much larger urban population. And another aspect: I honestly think the Chinese internet space isn't as hygienic or regulated. I could argue this is a Brave New World scenario, where the government actively wants to [unclear] people with that content.

That brings me to Namir's second question: Where are the great filmmakers in China? As a cinephile, I have to say, heartbreakingly, that the best Chinese artists and filmmaking practices emerged in the '90s and early 2000s. That was a relatively free China. I grew up in the early 2000s in China, and I think that was fundamental to my personality and how I view the world. It was a time when people had a lot of artistic freedom. People could criticize the government to a certain extent.

But recently I was chatting with a filmmaker who's still active in China. He said making a movie in China is like walking into a pitch-black room where, if you touch one piece of furniture, you die. So you need to move really, really slowly and feel where there might be a piece of furniture you don't want to touch. In the end, the only output in China is, for example, a drama where all the criminals have to surrender to the police at the end. The law makes it illegal to make movies that let criminals escape. That's just one of many, many examples of how Chinese censorship works.

Imagine you have so many imposed constraints. What's your creative space? What do you do? If I were in that pitch-black room, I wouldn't even move anymore, because I don't want to die. Moving forward, reaching for something, swinging my arms around could kill me. That's the situation with Chinese censorship, and it's why the Chinese entertainment industry isn't as prosperous as Korea's or Japan's: many filmmakers and artistic people are trapped in those dark rooms. The psychological effect is implicit. Imagine being in that dark room for decades. That's the result for the most creative minds in China. I think some of the best filmmakers are diaspora Chinese, people who aren't constrained by those dark rooms. That's my answer, but I really appreciate this question.

DAN: Yeah, it's a great question. And I think it's probably not direct censorship so much as what you're describing, a sort of self-censorship that comes through the conditions of the society. The dark room analogy is really helpful for understanding that. Awesome. Thank you, Afra.

AFRA: Thank you.

DAN: All right, Namir, let's switch gears. Afra, hang by, and if you have any questions for Namir, I'd love that too. Namir, give us your background, man. You also spent some time working in the film industry, but you're a big-ideas guy. Give us a quick sense of your background and trajectory.

NAMIR: Yeah, I also grew up a cinephile. I also grew up a Big Think fan, capital B, capital T, watching your videos. And I grew up loving consuming content and engaging with ideas that introduced me to perspectives and concepts I otherwise would never have encountered. I wanted to pursue a career that gave me the best of both worlds. My early career was predominantly in the US film industry, quote-unquote Hollywood, working for a variety of studios and their subsidiary production companies. I got to work on big Hollywood productions for directors like Ron Howard and Judd Apatow. That was a great cultural and practical education in how stories and media are actually put together in an industrial, commercial way.

I still have one foot in that world, working with production companies to help develop and finance projects that use stories as vehicles for ideas I think are big and important, and helping the people who come up with those ideas, whether they're scientists, philosophers, or academics, play a part in the creative process. I've also gotten involved in other mediums, including writing for publications that are interested in disseminating ideas that could be important for the future, and Big Think is certainly one of them. I've written a handful of articles for you over the last couple of years, and then you came to me with an idea to tackle a piece on the permanent underclass. That's what brought me into this issue.

DAN: That's awesome. I love how on these calls we discover all the different ways our paths overlap. Give us a sense of your exploration in this piece. If I understand it right, it kind of started with a meme: the permanent underclass, this idea that AI is going to create a permanent underclass going forward. Can you unpack that, and how was that the start of your reporting journey?

NAMIR: Yeah. Especially when I was writing this piece, I was present enough on tech Twitter, or tech X, to be aware of the phrase and concept of the permanent underclass. But almost every post I saw about it treated it as a sardonic joke: people saying that if you don't quit your job and start an AI startup tomorrow, you're going to be stuck in the permanent underclass. Obviously it was hinting at something, a lesser version that could be true, but taken to a hyperbolic extreme for humor. So in terms of the actual phrase and concept, I thought it really was just a joke.

So when you brought me the idea of a piece on the permanent underclass, I thought, how do I tell a story about something that's just a joke online? But I also kind of liked the challenge of figuring out how to write a piece about it. And even if I didn't necessarily believe there was a class of people truly worried about AI creating a permanent underclass, I thought there were tons of interesting trends, people, and ideas in the Bay Area and the US tech industry that circled around this idea. Every joke has some truth behind it. I was interested in exploring the whole milieu of what's going on in the modern US tech industry, where these concerns and ideas are coming from, and where a joke like this actually stems from. So I was eager to dive into that world and see what I could come up with.

In my first draft (we ended up editing this out of the final), I made allusions to one of my favorite stories, Joseph Conrad's novella Heart of Darkness. It's about an English officer in the colonial era who's assigned to go deep up a river into the Belgian Congo to find a man who has allegedly gone insane and is spewing all these crazy ideas about what the future entails and how the world works. So in my initial draft, I made a similar allusion: Just as that officer journeyed into the heart of darkness, I was journeying into the heart of the permanent underclass, making my way through Silicon Valley and encountering different characters and very challenging, provocative ideas. That was a motif I was thinking about as I went around the Bay Area having various conversations about what the future could hold at the intersection of AI, productivity, and purpose. I ended up having a fun journey and wrote a piece about it.

DAN: One of the things I value most about this, thinking about Big Think's values of open, thoughtful, curious, and constructive, is that it was a genuinely 360-degree look at the concept. You interviewed one of the guys who was making this joke regularly and ultimately had to say, "Hey guys, this is a joke," one of these Silicon Valley influencers. You interviewed a VC who's part of the tech elite. You interviewed "Midwestern Paul," an alias for a guy who'd lost his job, and a bunch of college students, and even more than that.

I was struck by Sahib Guladi, the sophomore at Stanford University. Genuinely, college kids, even at a place like Stanford, have this anxiety about the future and their role in it. They're like, "No, I don't want to be relegated to the permanent underclass." I imagine this was one of the things you discovered, where you realized, oh, this is actually a real thing. Can you talk specifically about Sahib and the vibe among college students?

One more point on this: I think everybody feels this to a certain extent. We just don't know how these tools are going to evolve, and we don't know what that means for our ability to create value in that future world. So the anxiety for college kids, especially ones shelling out hundreds of thousands of dollars to go to elite universities, is quite real. Talk a little about the real idea behind this.

NAMIR: Thinking back to my own time in college, that period of your life is one where you're really focused on yourself and developing yourself for the future. You're concerned about how to construct your life so you can sustain yourself for the rest of it. It's also a time when young people are perhaps most myopic and narrow-minded, seeing only what's immediately in front of them. For those reasons, both good and bad, the idea of a permanent underclass is most prevalent among people in that age range.

I think a place like Stanford is, for a couple of reasons, perhaps the university where you see it most starkly. Obviously there's its proximity to, and actual placement within, Silicon Valley. Literally across the street are some of the most prominent VC funds financing all the major AI labs and startups. Perhaps even more so, and Sahib himself pointed this out, Stanford is one of the most elite and hardest-to-get-into universities in the world, if not the most. People on track to get into Stanford, and who then actually do, have for years been told, and have come to understand themselves, that they're special and they're going to do well in the world. They have lots of opportunities and options for how to make their way. Whether they'll be economically viable isn't really a concern. Once you get into Stanford, you can have a bit of confidence that you'll do okay in life.

But then here comes this concept of the permanent underclass that threatens that self-conception. Combine how much you've come to see your future as hopefully special with how prevalent discussions about AI and its future impact are on Stanford's campus: how it could destroy humanity, create a utopia, all these things. The mix of all those forces has created a situation on that campus where, perhaps more than anywhere else in the US, fears of the permanent underclass are very real. What the permanent underclass means to you as a Stanford student is going to be very different from what it means to a blue-collar worker somewhere in middle America. And conversations about AI are 80% of your conversations, so of course you think AI is going to be incredibly deterministic in shaping what the future looks like, and thereby what your future looks like.

DAN: I want to ask you to define the term permanent underclass in a second. But just thinking out loud on the Stanford side: If you're a student for whom much of your self-worth is derived from achievement, academic performance, all of that, because that's the mindset you're in and you're trying to chart your course for the future, then it's like, if all of that is wiped away, what am I going to be left with? I think this is a good transition to the last couple of minutes of our conversation, about meaning, value, and purpose in the age of AI. But first, can you give us a definition of the permanent underclass for people who aren't familiar with the term?

NAMIR: In its most basic and commonly used definition, especially in the context of AI, it's the idea that artificial intelligence will create a situation where you can no longer climb the ladder of wealth and status by working your way up, because anything you could do as work, AI could just do better. That creates a situation where you're stuck with whatever capital you already have. If you have basically a subsistence level of capital, that's what you'll be stuck with, and you'll have no means to get out of that situation, rise to a higher status, or rise to a higher class. The entire idea of the American dream sort of evaporates.

On the other side of that line are the people with capital in an AI future: people heavily invested in frontier AI labs, people who own and control these models and the startups built around these technologies. That's going to be, by definition, a very small subset of the total population. And the people on each side of these lines are basically going to be locked into their positions forever, once AI matches and surpasses human ability in all domains. That's the basic fear.

The term itself originated in the 1960s, when academics were describing what was happening to blue-collar workers with the automation of blue-collar work and, in the following decades, the offshoring of those jobs. The fear was that people without white-collar skills, meaning service and knowledge skills, were going to be left in the dust. Unless something was intentionally done to help this class of people, they wouldn't have any means to pull themselves up by their bootstraps and find a productive place in society. So the term itself is old, but it has taken on new meaning and new valence in the modern world.

DAN: That's super interesting. I hadn't really heard it until I read the article, so it was useful to get the history. Okay, we'll just do one or two more. Also, everyone, if you have any questions for Afra or Namir, go ahead and drop them in. Claire, my colleague, is going to come on in a few minutes, and we'll pose some of your questions for the last little bit.

Similar to the Stanford question, in the article you ask whether the nation's character itself is built on the virtue of labor. America has this rugged spirit: coming over here in the first place, going out to the American West, charting our own course. That's a through line in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street too: Labor is important; you should work hard. You reference Nick Bostrom and a lot of his work, and it leaves us with the question: What happens if intelligent machines give us everything we could ever want? What's left in this AI-delivered utopia? What are we to do with ourselves? I think you cite Bostrom saying we'd get better at leisure, we'd enjoy music. Do you have any takeaways or thoughts on this? It's fundamentally changing how we think about work, and that's something that's going to affect all of us.

NAMIR: I'd be really curious to know whether the prospect of a world where traditional ways of making a living and finding purpose are no longer relevant is scarier to Americans than to people in other parts of the world. If there are people here from countries outside the US, I'd be curious to hear their perspective. As an American myself, that prospect is absolutely terrifying. I wouldn't know what to do with myself.

There are historical reasons for that. Many of the colonists who initially came over from Europe were Puritans, and their worldview has been hardwired into the fabric of American society. Combine that with the fact that America has always been rich in resources, both human and natural, and so has always been at the forefront of industry. There's always been a lot of opportunity to get ahead, and therefore you should get ahead. The AI race has thrown that into stark relief, because we're also the country leading the world, for now, on this technology, these models, and their opportunities. So in some ways, what's happening now with AI is supercharging the idea that if you want to make an impact during your brief time here on Earth, the way to do it is through labor and exertion and actually producing stuff.

So I think the idea of the permanent underclass is particularly scary in an American context. From what I can tell, most of the posts about it, even the jokes, are coming from Americans. Nick Bostrom is Swedish and comes from a somewhat more collectivist society. For him, I think the prospect of a world where you don't necessarily have a job isn't all that scary, because milder versions of that already exist in the Nordic countries and Northern Europe. It's not as stark to someone like him. Whereas there's going to have to be a transitional period, particularly for Americans, if we end up in a world where you don't get purpose through your labor.

That said, I don't think that's the world we're going to end up in. AI will impact the professional landscape significantly, but not in a fundamentally different way from previous technologies. I think it will end up on roughly the same level as the creation of computers and the internet, which, looking back, had massive impacts on society and specifically on the job market. Entire classes of jobs disappeared, but jobs themselves did not disappear. We found new things to do. That's the more optimistic perspective, and it's one I subscribe to.

I think the people most worried about AI being able to do everything are probably people for whom being on the computer and working with digital technologies is everything. But there is life beyond what we do on the computer. We'll find ways to be productive. We might need to reorient our conception of what "productive" means. Instead of what did I produce that day or that week, it might be what did I produce this year, or this decade, with the help of these technologies. In the long term, I'm not too concerned about whether we'll find things to do with ourselves. In the short term, there will be tons of disruption, and we'll need to work together to minimize that and make sure the hardship, whatever it is, isn't borne by one specific class or group of people. But I have hope for humanity.

DAN: Claire, if you want to pop on, we can go to some questions, and Afra, if you have anything else. But as we do, I'd also offer this: My colleague Dusty just walked by. He's a guy I've been working with for about 15 years, an amazing DP, lighting guy, director, and producer. We've been having this conversation, because even in filmmaking, we're sometimes switching toward lighting things flat and then doing the lighting work in post-production. That's kind of an assault on our identity. We took so much care for decades to light things in a particular way. It's a very human skill, one we've refined for many, many years. But AI tools really can take a scene and light it in new ways, and that gives us so much more flexibility.

So we're both like, "Oh man, that sucks. We're humans; we should do that." But we're also like, "Oh wait, we can just do all this in post. This is amazing." I think for so many people there's this mixed feeling, this paradox of progress and fear. It's a weird time to be alive in many ways. But Claire, what are we hearing in the chat? Do we have any questions?

CLAIRE: Yeah, we have one that maybe Namir could take. It's from Dr. Karen. She says, "I'm very interested in the paradox of AI reducing barriers and friction in some ways (AI as personal work support), while also creating or exacerbating friction in others: increasing cognitive load and burnout, and workplace loneliness and isolation as an outcome of AI use." She said she'd love others' thoughts, so Namir, if you have any thoughts on that.

NAMIR: I can speak to the loneliness aspect a bit. Especially among people who believe the permanent underclass could be real and is coming, maybe not in its most extreme form, but who believe AI is going to be epochal in its impact on the labor landscape: These are the people who have basically left their bigger, more social jobs and locked themselves in a room to vibe-code their way to an AI startup unicorn.

I talked to one of my friends who left his big tech job, along with a couple of other people he knows, and now stays home all day trying to build an AI startup. I talked to a couple of young kids who left college, again, to start their own AI startups. In part that's because they want to make a difference, but I think they also want to make an economic impact in their own lives. They think staying in college and having these traditional professional and educational experiences is a waste of time when you could be tenfold or a hundredfold more productive by locking yourself in your bedroom and using 100 AI agents at a time to create something you otherwise couldn't create through traditional means. So I think it will certainly create more atomization if people continue down this path of becoming reliant on AI.

DAN: I'm glad this is where we're landing as we get to a close, and Claire might have another couple of questions too. It comes back to meaning, value creation, and contribution. In an era of AI, is there a fundamental, innate need for human beings to contribute, to create value for other people? I mean, lying by the pool is cool, but I'd probably get tired of it by day two and be like, "Yo, let's go solve cancer, or make movies, or do something crazy." That's just my personal thought experiment. But Claire, what else have we got?

CLAIRE: We have one for Afra from Nathan. He said, "Given Afra's fascinating take on the allocation of computing priorities in China, does this suggest that American frontier AI companies have more opportunities to control the technology without fear of losing a nonexistent AI war?"

DAN: Good question.

AFRA: I think this question has two layers. The first layer is what those local governments want. You can think of Chinese local governments as American VCs. They're the ones pulling capital together, attracting talent, and empowering it. They're basically saying, "We'll provide you free workspace, a lot of compute, a lot of subsidies, a lot of tax reductions, if you bring a team to create strategic AI-generated content in our region. You'll be rewarded with this and that." So imagine those local governments as VCs. They want monetary returns. They want actual economic benefits. In that sense, a big part of Chinese compute gets allocated to the AI slop industry. From a profit-seeking perspective, that's what's happening in China.

The second layer is the US-China AI race. What exactly is the race? My verdict for a long time has been this: I think the US is participating in a race that's designed by China, and not 100% participating. In China, the race is a full-stack national capacity race. It means manufacturing. It means the ability to export. It means how reliable your supply chain is, and how many countries rely on China's supply chain. That's the strategic goal China is pursuing, and AI is part of that full-stack race. At the same time, there's the frontier AI race driven by Silicon Valley, which China isn't fully participating in.

So I think there are two races. One is designed by China, one is designed by the US, and both countries are asking, are we in this race or not? China's race is going extremely well, and US frontier AI is going well. I think the US is putting way too much attention on Chinese frontier AI development rather than on China's full-stack state capacity. So in a sense, the US-China AI race or AI war framework isn't very complete if you consider both countries' complex topology.

And if you get into the decision-makers' mental models, I have a theory I call the "mandate of AI." Who has the divine power to use AI to design a future society, to design the physical space? In China, it's the party, the state. It's not necessarily the people working in tech or the AI industry. In Xi Jinping's vision, in the CCP's vision, AI ought to be diffused into heavy industry, into the industries that the CCP and the beneficiaries of those industries control. Whereas in Silicon Valley, it's the entrepreneurs and the founders who have this divine mandate of AI. I think understanding that difference would bring more clarity to the US-China AI race.

DAN: Man, that sounds like another article you should probably write for Big Think, about the different layers of the China-versus-US AI race. With NVIDIA and Jensen Huang and all the stuff happening right now, this is a very important, critical topic to understand. What I appreciate about your writing and reporting is that you're adding a cultural layer to what otherwise feels like almost purely a national security race or a technology race. There's also a cultural aspect to how both countries are approaching AI, and I really appreciate you educating us on that. Thanks a lot for that contribution.

We're just about at time. I have one more question, and then I want to give you both an opportunity to shout out where people can follow you and find more of your work. Claire, I think you had one more question.

CLAIRE: This was a question within a comment, but I think it's a good one to end on: "I believe many people are intimidated by the question, 'What can I create that provides value to others and generates income in an AI-dominated world?'"

DAN: Either of you, I'm curious to get your take on that, and then we'll wrap it up.

NAMIR: I think the wrong answer, which my entire piece is sort of about, is to silo yourself with a handful of AI agents and just try to create value for yourself, whether that's an AI startup or an AI slop machine, and to do it in an individualized way, as opposed to creating something that has not only potential monetary value but actual social and humanistic value. I think AI has tons of opportunities to create those sorts of things as well. You might have to dig a little harder and partner with some people to do it, but I think that's the brighter side of the same coin.

DAN: Yeah, totally. What do you think, Afra? Do you have a thought on that one?

AFRA: My take is slightly cliché techno-optimist, and also a bit utilitarian and practical. Because I was born and raised in China, I witnessed China's economic miracle and how technology advanced people's standard of living. So I have this conviction, though I always cast doubt on it, that AI, the highest form of productive force (that Marxist term Xi Jinping always uses), shall prevail. I think a lot of disruptions and changes will happen. And how can you prevent that from happening in this capitalist market? The whole system is so devouring.

So I would say: Don't reject it. Give yourself more permission to try different tools, try different things, ask AI a lot of questions, try different models, and follow AI news. It's interesting, exciting, and terrifying, but you have to understand its nature. Give yourself permission to understand it. Be a little bit AGI-pilled, so you have a better cognitive framework to at least participate in the discussion about the future.

A lot of these discussions can be very unappealing. As we discussed, America has this evangelical Protestant culture where work is the highest of virtues. But there's also the high-level discourse in China. What are people saying about a potential intelligence explosion? What does the future utopia look like from Silicon Valley's perspective? If you don't agree with them, what's your version of dystopia or utopia? I think everyone should seriously think about this. But first, give yourself permission to understand AI.

DAN: Cool. I appreciate that; that's a helpful close. I see you dropped it in the chat: People can follow Afra's work on Concurrent, a newsletter exploring the colliding tech and cultural currents shaping Silicon Valley, China, and beyond. Thank you so much, Afra, for coming.

AFRA: Thank you.

DAN: And Namir, where can folks follow you? At Protostellar, your production company?

NAMIR: I think just look out for more of my stuff on Big Think in the near future, hopefully.

DAN: Okay, cool. And Protostellar Media is the science communication production company you run. Thank you both so much for all this. I think this was a really helpful, interesting discussion.

For the members who are still on, I think a lot of what's in this issue is really valuable, in particular Kristin Houser's rundown of the different philosophies in AI (oops, I can't see it because it's getting bright in here): the techno-optimists, the doomers, the effective accelerationists, the safety-first advocates. It's a breakdown of the landscape that I think is really helpful. So check out the print edition. Thank you so much for contributing, and thanks for coming by today. I appreciate the conversation, and we'll see you next time. Thanks!
content_text: Big Think hosted a live event on our latest issue, Made in Our Image, which explores the philosophies behind artificial intelligence and what they reveal about us. Executive Producer Dan Hayes sat down with the writers behind the magazine for a candid conversation about the human side of this century’s most consequential technology, along with a behind-the-scenes look at what went into making our favorite issue yet. DAN: .It's a real point of pride for us at Big Think to produce these quarterly magazines. It's amazing to have a real-life thing you can put on your nightstand or coffee table and read in the real world. The response has frankly been overwhelming since we started. We continue to find more and more people who value big ideas, who are yearning for an analog thought partner, if you will. So shout-out to the whole team who made this possible. Thank you, guys. You're the best.I have two awesome writers with me today, Afra Wang and Namir Khaliq. Here's what we're going to get into. I'm going to throw 10 or 15 questions at you, just so you have context for where we're going.We're going to start by learning about the AI-generated film Zombie Scavenger, and what Afra thought she was going to find exploring AI slop and AI content creation in China. At some point I want to ask Afra what the worst piece of slop she saw while reporting this story was. I want to talk a little about the relationship between censorship and art, and what AI slop might ultimately have to do with China's ghost cities. There's an interesting parallel that Afra draws in her story.We'll also talk through the relationship between Afra's AI slop article and Namir's permanent underclass piece, which I think have some overlapping themes. I'm going to share a little about my experiences with AI as a filmmaker for the group to consider. Then, with Namir, we're going to talk about the idea of a permanent underclass. Is it real, or just a meme on X? Is AI the new industrial revolution, this time for knowledge workers? Is every generation convinced it's living through the end of history? Is it evolutionarily harder for us humans to genuinely imagine real upsides?Is our nation's character, from Silicon Valley to Wall Street to the American West, built on the virtue of labor? What happens if intelligent machines give us everything we could ever want? What might there be left to do with our lives in an AI-delivered utopia? And the last one: Do humans have a basic need to contribute in order to find meaning in our lives?Those are some of the topics we're going to explore. You can also put your questions in the chat, and my colleague Claire is going to pop on toward the end to share them. This is your chance to engage with some super smart and interesting people, so please feel free to load us up with questions, and we'll hit a bunch of them toward the end of the hour.Thank you both so much for being with us today. Afra, I want to start with you. Can you give us your personal background, so people understand how you got into this space in the first place? And please be sure to touch on your brief, dreamlike internship in the film industry.AFRA: Yeah, of course. I've been a cinephile for as long as I can remember. So when some video generation tools emerged from the Chinese AI space, I got really interested and really excited. At that moment, the whole discourse about the US-China AI race was already happening, and OpenAI had abandoned their Sora project. If you remember Sora, there was a brief moment when everyone could use ChatGPT's newest video generation tools to generate a bunch of slop. One of the most memorable was Sam Altman stealing GPUs from a random shopping mall, if you remember that.I was really intrigued by the level of creativity AI video generation as a vertical could reach. At the same time, China seemed to have an advantage, in the sense that a lot more video generation tools were coming out of China's innovation space, and a lot more people seemed to want to jump into AI and creativity. Meanwhile, in the West, if you're a reputable director and you dare to say out loud, "I'm optimistic about AI, I want to embrace this technology," you'll probably get denounced by your peers, or feel morally delinquent, because a lot of people are protesting against AI. Unions in Hollywood are constantly organizing anti-AI activities.So I thought, okay, is this China's big opportunity to forge its own soft power through AI-generated content? That was my sort of 4D chess in my mind. I really wanted to understand this phenomenon, so I got into the space. I talked to many filmmakers, many producers, and many young people in their early 20s who had jumped into this space. I also watched a lot of AI slop myself. I downloaded a bunch of vertical short-video apps and spent hours and hours watching them, hoping to find something touching, something moving, something fundamentally artistic. What I found was this complex, this industrial-scale slop generation machine, which I wrote about in my article.As for my dream internship: I was a typical first-year college student who didn't know what to do over the summer. I was still a kid. I asked my mom, "If I spend two months in Beijing" (that's where I grew up, where my parents were) "what should I do?" My mom had some connections, and she got me into that internship. It was really fun. I was able to chat with a lot of Hong Kong directors. Beijing was a gold mountain back then. A lot of Hong Kong filmmakers, really the entire industry, were moving north and making Beijing a center of their artistic practice, so there was a big Hong Kong diaspora in Beijing. I was hanging out with a lot of those Hong Kong directors who had witnessed the most legendary phase of the golden age of Hong Kong cinema.DAN: That's awesome. That sounds like a pretty cool experience. So your hopes for AI film were high, given your background. Can you share the example of Zombie Scavenger? There have been glimmers of hope in what you've seen in China in terms of creativity, and you thought maybe this was the new way forward for AI. Tell people about that film and what happened after.AFRA: Yeah, absolutely. If you're familiar with Love, Death & Robots, the Netflix short series, Zombie Scavenger feels like one of those episodes. It's a very short piece, about three minutes, but the universe it brought me into was very real and very coherent. It's like how Love, Death & Robots gives you a complete story setting and invites you into a unique storytelling space: something happened in outer space, something happened in the future, something happened in a post-apocalyptic world. Zombie Scavenger is one of those stories. It takes place in a world where humans went extinct because of a zombie outbreak, and the whole story is a romance between a robot and a mannequin.It's really whimsical and romantic, and it has a lot of interesting motifs from '60s Hollywood movies, from the cowboy genre, and from the zombie genre. It really paid tribute to a lot of familiar motifs we all know. Then I learned that this short wasn't produced by one of those top-notch teams at Netflix. It was produced by a nobody, a 28-year-old nobody from Yunnan province. Not even Beijing or Shanghai, those cosmopolitan cities, but a very distant province. The filmmaker himself is a wedding photographer. He doesn't speak English; he didn't even make the film in English. But in the end, you get this Hollywood-quality output. That became huge news in the Chinese AI filmmaking industry.DAN: And real quick, Afra, you said it was produced in 10 days for $442. And it led to American filmmakers calling this kid and saying, "You should come and produce stuff with us." So this was a real moment in AI filmmaking.AFRA: Yeah, absolutely. The film became internationally renowned in a sense. Chinese AI filmmakers were very invigorated by it, and American filmmakers were thinking, okay, China is probably going to have an asymmetrical advantage. A lot more hidden talent is going to flourish because this tool lets people make something like this for a few hundred dollars. I was excited, a lot of Hollywood filmmakers were excited, and there was an effort to scout for talent from Hollywood. I personally know this filmmaker was contacted by a lot of Hollywood producers at the time, and many more young Chinese people were dreaming of being contacted by Hollywood filmmakers. So that was a very optimistic moment, and it got me started on this scavenger hunt through Chinese AI innovation in moviemaking.DAN: And so then you were like, all right, cool, let's go find all the other cool examples. But basically, you watched 15-plus AI films and tons more shorts, and you felt like you were in an uncanny valley that was terrible. What's some of the worst stuff you saw? And what makes this AI content actually slop? There are blurry lines, so why do you consider it slop?AFRA: Mostly, the reason you don't feel good after watching them is very similar to why you don't feel good after spending two hours scrolling TikTok. You've viscerally been hacked by the algorithm. Your dopamine is being depleted by the algorithm. While you're watching, you're hooked by very tacky, shocking, dramatic plots. Someone accidentally gets pregnant with a baby by both her husband and her husband's brother. There are certain elements of those dramas that are just subversively controversial and make you want to keep going. And the reason you want to keep going is not good. It's not your artistic curiosity or your intellectual curiosity. It's just that your dopamine has been hacked.You're like a monkey that's been fed one bite of banana and wants to chase the next bite. I really felt like an animal being harnessed by the algorithm to keep watching, and I honestly don't appreciate that feeling. All those AI slops don't have deliberate or thoughtful plotlines. The plotlines just maximize how much drama can happen within three or four minutes. Then you need to hit the next one, and three episodes later, you need to pay to keep watching.DAN: I feel like it's not necessarily slop, but even modern YouTube influencer content has a certain characteristic, and definitely a certain pace. As a filmmaker, I can see it's going so fast. There's no space, no breath, because they're just trying to give people that story hit, that bite, to keep propelling them through a narrative. When I watch even modern YouTubers, it's hypercut, and the shots are so quick that I feel assaulted, or just tired watching it. It's kind of crazy.That's super interesting. And you're saying they're creating this stuff at incredible scale, basically trying to find a hit that makes this economic engine for producing slop viable. Talk a little about the scale of this. Afterward, I want to chat about the ghost cities, and then we'll head over to Namir for a bit.AFRA: Totally. After you watch enough AI slop, you start to notice that a lot of the female and male faces are converging into a very similar shape. They have very similar layouts of noses and eyes and ears. All of a sudden you think, there must be a vast industry behind this, probably because of economic incentives. So I started to dig in, and, not entirely to my surprise, it's highly tied to China's regional competition.China has 30-plus provinces, and each province, whether economically advanced or not, wants a share of the most advanced technological development that the central government is signaling to the entire state. Since 2024, Xi Jinping himself has publicly announced many times that AI is going to diffuse into many industries in China. AI is what they call the highest-quality "productive force." This is a very Marxist term. It means electricity was once that, energy was once that, and now it's AI. So Beijing sent a very clear signal to all the local governments and entrepreneurs that AI will be the thing that fuels the engine of China's innovation.This is basically how China works: Beijing sends out a signal and lets the local governments interpret it and figure out what it means. After the AI Plus initiative was announced, many local governments started to think, okay, how can we participate in this new innovation, this industrial upgrade? How can we not be left behind? How can we have a piece of this strategic technology when we don't have enough talent?I'm not talking about Beijing, Shanghai, or Shenzhen. Those advanced coastal cities were already participating in the AI revolution. I'm talking about many distant provinces and regions. One example would be Nanjing. It's a city with a large population, but nobody really sees Nanjing as a tech hub or AI hub. There's Hefei. There are many second-tier and third-tier cities saying, okay, we want to jump on this AI bandwagon and create a strategic AI initiative in our region. But what can we do that has the lowest barrier to entry? That's AI video generation. You can just get some compute, get a bunch of young people, plant some seeds in their minds, and have them be creative.That's an easy, participatory action a local government can take. So many governments started talent incubation programs, where they held public AI video generation competitions to attract people to submit their work and start their own studios. The local government would then give them subsidies or rewards to make the whole space more prosperous and popular. The whole industrial AI slop complex was pretty much a result of this regional competition among different local governments in China.DAN: So that's one of the reasons there's been such scale and volume in producing this AI slop. By the way, this is all totally new to me. I had no context for the Chinese cultural and policy side of this, so this was a really good educational article. Last question for you, and then, Namir, we'll head your way. You compare this to the ghost cities in China, these huge cities that were built at massive scale but are now empty and full of weeds. Help us understand that analogy.AFRA: I think it goes back to the downside of regional competition. China's regional competition has its own merits. The reason China is winning the EV race, the reason China was able to produce so many solar panels, the reason China was able to generate so much electricity and harness so much solar and hydropower, is that different regions compete against each other. They want a strategic advantage in certain important industries.At the same time, you have a very severe issue called overcapacity. Overcapacity is essentially something like a ghost city, where local officials were convinced that building infrastructure was fundamentally important. It's their way of getting promoted, of showing they're diligent civil servants, of being part of China's economic miracle. So everyone started building infrastructure, building cities, inviting real estate developers, and lending a bunch of money for those projects. In the end, China has a tremendous number of unoccupied, vacant high-rise buildings and residential complexes that nobody was able to afford or buy. And right now in China, the real estate bubble has burst too, so the ghost city scenario is even more severe. You drive to the suburbs and see a brand-new city appear in front of you, but it doesn't have many people.The exact same thing happened with China's high-speed railways. Today, 80% to 85% of Chinese high-speed rail lines are losing money, because many were built to connect distant cities to other distant cities, and there isn't enough traffic to cover the cost.And the exact same thing happened in AI slop generation. After all this talent and compute and local subsidies poured into the space, you get a tremendous amount of content that nobody is watching. If you understand the YouTube or TikTok algorithms, you know they follow a power law. The top tier of creators, the 1%, occupy maybe 90% of people's attention. The same thing happened on those short-form AI video platforms. The result is a tremendous amount of stuff being produced that nobody watches, and people trying to squeeze out that 1% of good content and replicate it. So you see this homogenizing tendency, where all the characters look very similar, because a similar face was probably in one of the hits from two months ago, and they're trying to replicate that exact face in the next plotline. All these weird, uncanny things happen, and it just isn't a pleasant experience. In the end, I felt like I was venturing into many, many ghost cities. It's just not very good. I think I wrote this out of some slop PTSD. I got really overwhelmed. I wanted a mental cleanse.DAN: You've got to go watch some classic old films. Watch 8½ by Fellini or something, get yourself out of there. I thought it was really interesting. First of all, I think we should solve the US housing crisis by airlifting China's ghost cities into the US. I don't know if that would work, but maybe if we get big enough ships. But no, this article is awesome. The industrial slop complex, and the design is really cool. So if you members have your magazines, check out Afra's awesome article. Thank you so much, Afra, for educating us on this. It was really, really cool.AFRA: Thank you so much, Dan.NAMIR: Can I jump in with a final question? One: Who is watching this sort of stuff in China? Is it young people? Old people? Everyone? No one? And two: Do you have a theory as to why China hasn't been able to develop the same sort of international cultural reputation as even South Korea or Japan, let alone the US? Do they just not have the same internal culture developed as these other places, or what's the cause?AFRA: I'll answer the first question first: Who's watching AI slop? Everyone, from 70-year-old grandpas to 15-year-old high schoolers. If there's a US-China AI race, I think the US and China are also racing to brain-rot each other's populations. And if there's a brain-rot race, China is probably winning right now.A couple of weeks ago, there was a huge debate online about compute usage in China versus the US. Some argued that half of Chinese compute goes to AI slop generation, while a lot of US compute goes to R&D, software programming, and AI for science. In the highbrow Chinese AI discussion sphere, people were paranoid about China's overwhelming amount of AI slop, asking: Are we losing our grip? Are we losing our advantage? Why are we using so much compute and inference just to feed AI slop? People in the Chinese AI industry are even having an identity crisis, which I found really interesting.If you go to China, you'll see that people are a lot more addicted to digital life. People are a lot more interested in going to Instagrammable restaurants, taking pictures, and posting them on social media. That whole activity is much more prevalent. I think that's partly because China has a much larger urban population. And another aspect: I honestly think the Chinese internet space isn't as hygienic or regulated. I could argue this is a Brave New World scenario, where the government actively wants to [unclear] people with that content.That brings me to Namir's second question: Where are the great filmmakers in China? As a cinephile, I have to say, heartbreakingly, that the best Chinese artists and filmmaking practices emerged in the '90s and early 2000s. That was a relatively free China. I grew up in the early 2000s in China, and I think that was fundamental to my personality and how I view the world. It was a time when people had a lot of artistic freedom. People could criticize the government to a certain extent.But recently I was chatting with a filmmaker who's still active in China. He said making a movie in China is like walking into a pitch-black room where, if you touch one piece of furniture, you die. So you need to move really, really slowly and feel where there might be a piece of furniture you don't want to touch. In the end, the only output in China is, for example, a drama where all the criminals have to surrender to the police at the end. The law makes it illegal to make movies that let criminals escape. That's just one of many, many examples of how Chinese censorship works.Imagine you have so many imposed constraints. What's your creative space? What do you do? If I were in that pitch-black room, I wouldn't even move anymore, because I don't want to die. Moving forward, reaching for something, swinging my arms around could kill me. That's the situation with Chinese censorship, and it's why the Chinese entertainment industry isn't as prosperous as Korea's or Japan's: many filmmakers and artistic people are trapped in those dark rooms. The psychological effect is implicit. Imagine being in that dark room for decades. That's the result for the most creative minds in China. I think some of the best filmmakers are diaspora Chinese, people who aren't constrained by those dark rooms. That's my answer, but I really appreciate this question.DAN: Yeah, it's a great question. And I think it's probably not direct censorship so much as what you're describing, a sort of self-censorship that comes through the conditions of the society. The dark room analogy is really helpful for understanding that. Awesome. Thank you, Afra.AFRA: Thank you.DAN: All right, Namir, let's switch gears. Afra, hang by, and if you have any questions for Namir, I'd love that too. Namir, give us your background, man. You also spent some time working in the film industry, but you're a big-ideas guy. Give us a quick sense of your background and trajectory.NAMIR: Yeah, I also grew up a cinephile. I also grew up a Big Think fan, capital B, capital T, watching your videos. And I grew up loving consuming content and engaging with ideas that introduced me to perspectives and concepts I otherwise would never have encountered. I wanted to pursue a career that gave me the best of both worlds. My early career was predominantly in the US film industry, quote-unquote Hollywood, working for a variety of studios and their subsidiary production companies. I got to work on big Hollywood productions for directors like Ron Howard and Judd Apatow. That was a great cultural and practical education in how stories and media are actually put together in an industrial, commercial way.I still have one foot in that world, working with production companies to help develop and finance projects that use stories as vehicles for ideas I think are big and important, and helping the people who come up with those ideas, whether they're scientists, philosophers, or academics, play a part in the creative process. I've also gotten involved in other mediums, including writing for publications that are interested in disseminating ideas that could be important for the future, and Big Think is certainly one of them. I've written a handful of articles for you over the last couple of years, and then you came to me with an idea to tackle a piece on the permanent underclass. That's what brought me into this issue.DAN: That's awesome. I love how on these calls we discover all the different ways our paths overlap. Give us a sense of your exploration in this piece. If I understand it right, it kind of started with a meme: the permanent underclass, this idea that AI is going to create a permanent underclass going forward. Can you unpack that, and how was that the start of your reporting journey?NAMIR: Yeah. Especially when I was writing this piece, I was present enough on tech Twitter, or tech X, to be aware of the phrase and concept of the permanent underclass. But almost every post I saw about it treated it as a sardonic joke: people saying that if you don't quit your job and start an AI startup tomorrow, you're going to be stuck in the permanent underclass. Obviously it was hinting at something, a lesser version that could be true, but taken to a hyperbolic extreme for humor. So in terms of the actual phrase and concept, I thought it really was just a joke.So when you brought me the idea of a piece on the permanent underclass, I thought, how do I tell a story about something that's just a joke online? But I also kind of liked the challenge of figuring out how to write a piece about it. And even if I didn't necessarily believe there was a class of people truly worried about AI creating a permanent underclass, I thought there were tons of interesting trends, people, and ideas in the Bay Area and the US tech industry that circled around this idea. Every joke has some truth behind it. I was interested in exploring the whole milieu of what's going on in the modern US tech industry, where these concerns and ideas are coming from, and where a joke like this actually stems from. So I was eager to dive into that world and see what I could come up with.In my first draft (we ended up editing this out of the final), I made allusions to one of my favorite stories, Joseph Conrad's novella Heart of Darkness. It's about an English officer in the colonial era who's assigned to go deep up a river into the Belgian Congo to find a man who has allegedly gone insane and is spewing all these crazy ideas about what the future entails and how the world works. So in my initial draft, I made a similar allusion: Just as that officer journeyed into the heart of darkness, I was journeying into the heart of the permanent underclass, making my way through Silicon Valley and encountering different characters and very challenging, provocative ideas. That was a motif I was thinking about as I went around the Bay Area having various conversations about what the future could hold at the intersection of AI, productivity, and purpose. I ended up having a fun journey and wrote a piece about it.DAN: One of the things I value most about this, thinking about Big Think's values of open, thoughtful, curious, and constructive, is that it was a genuinely 360-degree look at the concept. You interviewed one of the guys who was making this joke regularly and ultimately had to say, "Hey guys, this is a joke," one of these Silicon Valley influencers. You interviewed a VC who's part of the tech elite. You interviewed "Midwestern Paul," an alias for a guy who'd lost his job, and a bunch of college students, and even more than that.I was struck by Sahib Guladi, the sophomore at Stanford University. Genuinely, college kids, even at a place like Stanford, have this anxiety about the future and their role in it. They're like, "No, I don't want to be relegated to the permanent underclass." I imagine this was one of the things you discovered, where you realized, oh, this is actually a real thing. Can you talk specifically about Sahib and the vibe among college students?One more point on this: I think everybody feels this to a certain extent. We just don't know how these tools are going to evolve, and we don't know what that means for our ability to create value in that future world. So the anxiety for college kids, especially ones shelling out hundreds of thousands of dollars to go to elite universities, is quite real. Talk a little about the real idea behind this.NAMIR: Thinking back to my own time in college, that period of your life is one where you're really focused on yourself and developing yourself for the future. You're concerned about how to construct your life so you can sustain yourself for the rest of it. It's also a time when young people are perhaps most myopic and narrow-minded, seeing only what's immediately in front of them. For those reasons, both good and bad, the idea of a permanent underclass is most prevalent among people in that age range.I think a place like Stanford is, for a couple of reasons, perhaps the university where you see it most starkly. Obviously there's its proximity to, and actual placement within, Silicon Valley. Literally across the street are some of the most prominent VC funds financing all the major AI labs and startups. Perhaps even more so, and Sahib himself pointed this out, Stanford is one of the most elite and hardest-to-get-into universities in the world, if not the most. People on track to get into Stanford, and who then actually do, have for years been told, and have come to understand themselves, that they're special and they're going to do well in the world. They have lots of opportunities and options for how to make their way. Whether they'll be economically viable isn't really a concern. Once you get into Stanford, you can have a bit of confidence that you'll do okay in life.But then here comes this concept of the permanent underclass that threatens that self-conception. Combine how much you've come to see your future as hopefully special with how prevalent discussions about AI and its future impact are on Stanford's campus: how it could destroy humanity, create a utopia, all these things. The mix of all those forces has created a situation on that campus where, perhaps more than anywhere else in the US, fears of the permanent underclass are very real. What the permanent underclass means to you as a Stanford student is going to be very different from what it means to a blue-collar worker somewhere in middle America. And conversations about AI are 80% of your conversations, so of course you think AI is going to be incredibly deterministic in shaping what the future looks like, and thereby what your future looks like.DAN: I want to ask you to define the term permanent underclass in a second. But just thinking out loud on the Stanford side: If you're a student for whom much of your self-worth is derived from achievement, academic performance, all of that, because that's the mindset you're in and you're trying to chart your course for the future, then it's like, if all of that is wiped away, what am I going to be left with? I think this is a good transition to the last couple of minutes of our conversation, about meaning, value, and purpose in the age of AI. But first, can you give us a definition of the permanent underclass for people who aren't familiar with the term?NAMIR: In its most basic and commonly used definition, especially in the context of AI, it's the idea that artificial intelligence will create a situation where you can no longer climb the ladder of wealth and status by working your way up, because anything you could do as work, AI could just do better. That creates a situation where you're stuck with whatever capital you already have. If you have basically a subsistence level of capital, that's what you'll be stuck with, and you'll have no means to get out of that situation, rise to a higher status, or rise to a higher class. The entire idea of the American dream sort of evaporates.On the other side of that line are the people with capital in an AI future: people heavily invested in frontier AI labs, people who own and control these models and the startups built around these technologies. That's going to be, by definition, a very small subset of the total population. And the people on each side of these lines are basically going to be locked into their positions forever, once AI matches and surpasses human ability in all domains. That's the basic fear.The term itself originated in the 1960s, when academics were describing what was happening to blue-collar workers with the automation of blue-collar work and, in the following decades, the offshoring of those jobs. The fear was that people without white-collar skills, meaning service and knowledge skills, were going to be left in the dust. Unless something was intentionally done to help this class of people, they wouldn't have any means to pull themselves up by their bootstraps and find a productive place in society. So the term itself is old, but it has taken on new meaning and new valence in the modern world.DAN: That's super interesting. I hadn't really heard it until I read the article, so it was useful to get the history. Okay, we'll just do one or two more. Also, everyone, if you have any questions for Afra or Namir, go ahead and drop them in. Claire, my colleague, is going to come on in a few minutes, and we'll pose some of your questions for the last little bit.Similar to the Stanford question, in the article you ask whether the nation's character itself is built on the virtue of labor. America has this rugged spirit: coming over here in the first place, going out to the American West, charting our own course. That's a through line in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street too: Labor is important; you should work hard. You reference Nick Bostrom and a lot of his work, and it leaves us with the question: What happens if intelligent machines give us everything we could ever want?
